key_points.text: Abstraction means removing details that aren't needed, so a problem becomes simpler to understand and solve. You may be asked how abstraction has been applied to a scenario, how it could be applied, or how it could be taken further.

Abstraction is needed because real situations are too complex to model fully: it reduces the processing, memory and programming effort needed, makes the solution easier to design and understand, and lets you focus on the core problem.

An abstraction differs from reality because details have been removed or simplified. Exam questions often ask what has been left out and why (for example, a route-planning model might ignore scenery, weather and road surface).
To devise an abstract model: decide what the problem needs to know, keep only those features, and represent them simply (for example, a graph of nodes and weighted edges for a road network).
Abstraction appears throughout computing: high-level languages hide machine code, the TCP/IP layers hide the layers beneath them, and subroutines hide how a task is done.

dont_confuse.text: Abstraction vs decomposition: abstraction removes unnecessary detail; decomposition splits a problem into smaller parts. You usually use both.
